01 / AN ATHLETE'S QUESTION. AN ANALYST'S APPROACH.

Predicting the Podium.

Can machine learning predict the podium finishers at the 2026 World Aquatics Swimming Championships (25m) in Beijing?

Having spent 14 years in competitive swimming, including four years representing Sri Lanka on the national team, I know how unpredictable a race can be. Months of preparation can come down to a fraction of a second, and even the favourites don't always finish first.

This inspired me to explore a question through my background in Business Analytics: How much of a swimming race can we actually predict using data?

For this independent research project, I analysed results from five previous World Short Course Championships and six recent World Cup meets. Using machine learning and statistical simulations, I investigated how age, competitive experience, recent form and historical performances relate to race times and potential medal outcomes across 36 individual events.

This project brings together two of my biggest interests: understanding swimming as an athlete and uncovering patterns through data.

02 / THE STORY BEHIND THE RESEARCH

From Athlete to Analyst.

Swimming shaped my childhood. My passion for it never left, it simply found a new direction.

Where it all began

Swimming has been one of the biggest parts of my life for as long as I can remember. I spent around 14 years in the sport, with eight of those years dedicated to competitive swimming. Waking up at 4 in the morning, getting into freezing cold water before sunrise and spending hours training was just a normal part of growing up for me.

I had the privilege of representing Sri Lanka internationally, including at BIMSTEC Youth Water Sports and a competition in Malaysia. I was also part of the Sri Lankan National Swimming Team from 2021 to 2024. Swimming taught me discipline, determination and how much effort goes into improving even by a fraction of a second.

A new chapter

Throughout school, I balanced competitive swimming with academics, managing early morning training and competitions while maintaining strong results in my studies. When I moved to Australia for university, I stepped away from competitive swimming to focus on my education. Although it was a big change, swimming has always remained an important part of my life.

I graduated from Monash University with a Bachelor of Commerce, majoring in Business Analytics with minors in Finance and Economics. My interest in machine learning and Sports Economics inspired me to explore swimming from a different perspective.

Where Swimming Meets Machine Learning

Having competed for so many years, I know the fastest swimmer on paper does not always win. I wanted to use previous championship results and recent performances to explore who might finish first, second and third in Beijing. That is how Predicting the Podium began. It brings together what I learned at university and a sport I have loved since childhood.

03 / DEFINING THE RESEARCH PROBLEM

Seven Questions. One Finish Line.

≋   What exactly am I trying to predict?

Predicting a swimming race is not as simple as choosing the swimmer with the fastest personal best. Athletes improve, performances fluctuate, and someone who dominated last season might not necessarily perform the same way at the next championship.

For Beijing 2026, I wanted to go beyond predicting individual winners. My goal was to investigate whether machine learning could estimate race times, identify medal contenders and eventually predict gold, silver and bronze in the correct finishing order across 36 individual events.

◎   The Seven Research Questions

01

Race Time Prediction

Can historical performances and recent results help predict how fast each swimmer will race?

02

Age & Experience

At what ages do elite swimmers tend to perform best, and does this vary between strokes and distances?

03

Recent Form vs Past Success

Are recent World Cup performances more useful than results from previous World Championships?

04

Long Course vs Short Course

Can performances from the Olympics (50m pools) help predict results in short course racing (25m pools)?

05

Emerging Talent

Can the model identify improving swimmers who might challenge established champions?

06

Model Reliability

Which machine learning approach produces the most accurate race time forecasts and, with further validation, the most reliable medal probabilities?

07

The Final Podium

Can the model predict not just the three medallists, but their exact finishing order?

  How I approached
the problem
01 · COLLECTBring together historical championship results and recent World Cup data.
02 · UNDERSTANDExamine age, previous performances, experience and event characteristics.
03 · BUILD & TESTCompare machine learning models and evaluate forecasts against a held out championship.
04 · PREDICTExplore potential podiums using race times and statistical simulations.
⚑   The ultimate goal:Can we move from knowing who has swum the fastest to understanding who is most likely to finish first, second and third when it matters?

05 / THE HUMAN VARIABLES

Age, Experience & Progression.

A swimmer is more than one finish time. Development, age, championships contested, recent racing frequency and consistency may influence performance, but they must be measured carefully.

  Age and Performance

Approximate age distribution of the current candidate field

Age describes the candidate pool. It does not establish that any age causes faster performances.

  Experience and Performance

Number of recent World Cup meets recorded per swimmer and event

One meet offers a useful time, but repeated races are needed to assess consistency.

  What the data can tell us

Age profiles

Compare athletes across age bands without claiming a universal peak age.

Championship experience

Earlier championship appearances are included in the historical models.

Progression

Recent times show whether a swimmer's form is changing across recorded meets.

Consistency

Most estimates have only one recent meet, so consistency remains difficult to judge.

↗   Progression Over Time

An actual recent World Cup series: Gretchen Walsh, Women's 50m Butterfly

Individual performances fluctuate. A few meets are a descriptive record, not a confirmed performance trend or a causal age effect.
ⓘ   Takeaway:Age, experience and improvement are worth studying together. Their separate effects are not yet isolated in this research.
06 / THE MODELLING APPROACH

Turning Data into Podium Predictions.

I compared historical machine learning models to forecast race times, then used a separate simulation based on recent World Cup results to explore possible medal outcomes for Beijing 2026.

  The Modelling Pipeline

01Data inputHistorical championship and World Cup results
02Feature engineeringBuild athlete, event and past performance features
03Model developmentTrain and compare historical race time models
04EvaluationEvaluate performance using the 2024 holdout
05Exploratory simulationEstimate medal chances under assumed time variation

  Machine Learning Models

Three approaches reported in the supplied R research

Linear RegressionA statistical baseline for interpreting the relationship between selected predictors and race time changes.
Random ForestCombines decision trees to capture more complex patterns in historical performances.
Gradient BoostingBuilds successive models to improve predictions from historical performance features.
Historical features include age, championship experience, event details and earlier race times.

  Model Performance Comparison

What this does and does not prove

Historical testing supports the race time modelling comparison. It does not validate the Beijing medal probabilities, which use World Cup best times and 10,000 simulated races per event and scenario.

08 / THE RESULT BEYOND THE RACE

What Did I Learn?

Building a prediction is only part of the work. Explaining what it can and cannot support is equally important.

01

History offers a baseline

Gradient Boosting reached 1.455% MAPE and 1.32 second MAE on the reported 2024 historical holdout.

02

One result is not a trend

3,566 of 4,505 swimmer event estimates use one World Cup meet, limiting recent form consistency analysis.

03

The field itself is uncertain

The included swimmers are data derived contenders, not independently verified event entrants.

04

Probabilities are assumptions

Changing race time variation changes medal chances. The simulation does not yet establish real world calibration.

05

A surprising medal is possible

A swimmer outside the three fastest baseline times may still receive a meaningful simulated podium chance.

06

Age must be interpreted carefully

Age and experience are useful model candidates; their isolated effect on performance remains untested here.

  Where could an outsider surprise us?

Strongest simulated any medal probability outside the three fastest baselines, by selected event

Outsider means outside the fastest three in the source dataset, not an unseeded or unqualified swimmer. Estimates may change with official entries.

  What is still missing?

01Official individual entriesConfirm the Beijing field and remove non entrants before assessing forecasts.
02Better longitudinal coverageAdd verified birth dates, championship appearances, progression and newer performances.
03Cross course validationTest paired Olympic 50m results against specific short course models.
04Medal probability calibrationBacktest probabilities and exact ordered podiums against completed competitions.
MY FINAL REFLECTION

The race doesn't end with a model prediction.

Swimming taught me to respect every detail that contributes to a result. Building this project taught me the same lesson about data: meaningful insights depend on clean sources, carefully designed tests and an honest account of what is uncertain. It gave me a way to stay connected to the sport I love while putting my machine learning skills to work on a question that matters personally to me.
